variants.title: Name the intermediary
variants.context: A forward proxy represents clients; a reverse proxy represents services. Layer 4 balancing sees addresses, ports, and connection state; Layer 7 parses the application protocol and can route by path, normalize headers, observe status codes, and retry only where the contract allows.
variants.prompt: An organization routes all outbound employee traffic through an intermediary that allows or denies destinations. Which is it?
options: A Layer 7 load balancer.
A forward proxy representing clients.
A reverse proxy representing services.
optionFeedback: It balances nothing.
The client side chose it for egress policy and identity.
Reverse proxies sit in front of services.
variants.hint: Who chose the proxy, and whom does it represent?
variants.explanation: “Forward” and “reverse” describe placement and owner; “load balancer” describes one job.

variants.title: Name the intermediary
variants.context: A forward proxy represents clients; a reverse proxy represents services. Layer 4 balancing sees addresses, ports, and connection state; Layer 7 parses the application protocol and can route by path, normalize headers, observe status codes, and retry only where the contract allows.
variants.prompt: A balancer only sees TCP connections and cannot read the encrypted HTTP path. Which layer is it?
options: Application gateway.
Layer 4.
Layer 7.
optionFeedback: A gateway implies L7 policy.
L4 routes flows by addresses, ports, and connection state.
L7 would parse the application protocol.
variants.hint: Can it read the request path?
variants.explanation: An L4 proxy is protocol-agnostic and blind to method, path, cookie, and status.

variants.title: Name the intermediary
variants.context: A forward proxy represents clients; a reverse proxy represents services. Layer 4 balancing sees addresses, ports, and connection state; Layer 7 parses the application protocol and can route by path, normalize headers, observe status codes, and retry only where the contract allows.
variants.prompt: Routing by host and path, normalizing headers, and retrying only idempotent methods require which layer?
options: Layer 4.
Either.
Layer 7.
optionFeedback: L4 cannot see paths or methods.
Only L7 can apply request policy.
Those policies need the application protocol parsed.
variants.hint: Which policies need the request parsed?
variants.explanation: L7 can retry only where the application contract allows.

variants.title: Trust each hop deliberately
variants.context: A proxy splits the path into separate downstream and upstream connections. Headers arriving directly from the client are untrusted; the trusted edge strips reserved identity fields and writes canonical values; later hops accept them only from known peers.
variants.prompt: A request carries a forged X-Forwarded-For. Put the trusted path in order.

items.text: The trusted edge strips reserved identity fields and writes a canonical request ID and forwarding values.
The backend authenticates the asserted identity, authorizes, and enforces idempotency.
The balancer builds an eligible set from discovery, readiness, and policy, then picks a backend.
Telemetry correlates the request ID across attempts with bounded, credential-free dimensions.
The client supplies request bytes; any forwarding or identity header from it is untrusted input.

variants.hint: Canonical metadata is created once, at the first trusted edge.
variants.explanation: Later hops consume identity only from known peers; the forged header never survives the edge.

variants.title: Trust each hop deliberately
variants.context: A proxy splits the path into separate downstream and upstream connections. Headers arriving directly from the client are untrusted; the trusted edge strips reserved identity fields and writes canonical values; later hops accept them only from known peers.
variants.prompt: A tenant header must reach the backend safely. Put the steps in order.

items.text: The backend accepts the tenant only because it came from the trusted edge, then authorizes.
The balancer chooses a ready backend.
The client’s own tenant header is treated as untrusted.
Telemetry records route, target, and outcome without credentials.
The edge removes caller-supplied reserved fields and writes the canonical tenant from authenticated identity.

variants.hint: Identity headers are ordinary bytes unless the receiver knows who wrote them.
variants.explanation: Bind identity headers to a trusted hop; accept them on later hops only from allowlisted proxies.

variants.title: Trust each hop deliberately
variants.context: A proxy splits the path into separate downstream and upstream connections. Headers arriving directly from the client are untrusted; the trusted edge strips reserved identity fields and writes canonical values; later hops accept them only from known peers.
variants.prompt: PROXY protocol is being enabled. Put the safe rollout in order.

items.text: Backends accept it from the allowlisted proxy addresses only.
The application authorizes using the canonical values.
The edge writes canonical source metadata.
Confirm the receiver expects PROXY protocol only from that transport peer.

variants.hint: PROXY protocol has the same trust rule as forwarding headers.
variants.explanation: Enable it only when the receiver expects it from that peer; otherwise a client can forge source identity.

variants.title: Define TLS ownership
variants.context: Pass-through keeps end-to-end TLS but prevents HTTP-aware inspection. Termination decrypts at the proxy; plaintext upstream belongs only inside a documented controlled network. Termination and re-encryption creates two TLS trust relationships.
variants.prompt: The proxy must route by HTTP path, and the backend must still be reached over TLS. Which mode?
options: Termination and re-encryption at the proxy.
Pass-through so TLS stays end to end.
Termination with a plaintext hop upstream.
optionFeedback: Decrypt for L7 policy, then verify a separate backend certificate.
Pass-through keeps the bytes encrypted, so the proxy cannot read the path it must route on.
Plaintext upstream is only for a documented controlled network.
variants.hint: Which mode lets the proxy read the path and still encrypt upstream?
variants.explanation: Name both trust relationships; they are not one end-to-end session.

variants.title: Define TLS ownership
variants.context: Pass-through keeps end-to-end TLS but prevents HTTP-aware inspection. Termination decrypts at the proxy; plaintext upstream belongs only inside a documented controlled network. Termination and re-encryption creates two TLS trust relationships.
variants.prompt: The backend must own the certificate and see the original encrypted bytes. Which mode?
options: Re-encryption.
Pass-through.
Termination.
optionFeedback: Re-encryption still decrypts at the proxy.
The proxy forwards encrypted bytes; the backend owns plaintext.
Termination moves plaintext to the proxy.
variants.explanation: Pass-through preserves end-to-end TLS but prevents inspection at the proxy.

variants.title: Define TLS ownership
variants.context: Pass-through keeps end-to-end TLS but prevents HTTP-aware inspection. Termination decrypts at the proxy; plaintext upstream belongs only inside a documented controlled network. Termination and re-encryption creates two TLS trust relationships.
variants.prompt: A proxy terminates TLS and forwards plaintext across a shared cloud network. What is missing?
options: A documented controlled network, or re-encryption.
Nothing; TLS termination at the edge is standard.
A longer certificate lifetime on the proxy.
optionFeedback: Plaintext upstream belongs only inside a documented controlled network.
Termination is fine. The unprotected plaintext hop after it is the risk.
Certificate lifetime changes rotation work, not who can read the plaintext hop.
variants.explanation: Termination is a placement decision with a network-trust assumption attached.

variants.title: Choose the signal
variants.context: An algorithm maps a signal to a target. Round robin for similar targets; least connections for long L4 sessions; least active requests for L7 duration differences; power of two choices for low-coordination least-load; consistent hash for affinity. Affinity concentrates hot keys and can pin callers to a degraded target.
variants.prompt: Backends use HTTP/2, and least connections keeps sending work to one target. Why, and what is better?
options: Switch to round robin so every target gets equal work.
Raise the weight on the other targets.
Connection count misleads; use least active requests.
optionFeedback: Equal shares ignore load entirely, so a loaded target keeps receiving its full rotation.
Weights encode static capacity, not live load, so the skew returns as traffic shifts.
Outstanding L7 requests reflect work better than connection count under multiplexing.
variants.hint: How many requests can one connection carry?
variants.explanation: Choose an algorithm only after choosing a useful load signal.

variants.title: Choose the signal
variants.context: An algorithm maps a signal to a target. Round robin for similar targets; least connections for long L4 sessions; least active requests for L7 duration differences; power of two choices for low-coordination least-load; consistent hash for affinity. Affinity concentrates hot keys and can pin callers to a degraded target.
variants.prompt: A global least-load scan is too expensive across thousands of targets. Which approach keeps most of the benefit?
options: Sticky sessions so each client stays put.
Power of two choices: sample two and pick the lighter.
Random selection across the whole target set.
optionFeedback: Affinity answers a different question and never compares load between targets.
Two samples get much of the benefit with low coordination cost.
Uniform random spreads work but never looks at load, so a hot target stays hot.
variants.hint: How much information do you need to avoid the worst target?
variants.explanation: Power of two choices is a well-studied trade of coordination for balance.

variants.title: Choose the signal
variants.context: An algorithm maps a signal to a target. Round robin for similar targets; least connections for long L4 sessions; least active requests for L7 duration differences; power of two choices for low-coordination least-load; consistent hash for affinity. Affinity concentrates hot keys and can pin callers to a degraded target.
variants.prompt: Client-IP affinity keeps users pinned to a degraded target. What is the better design?
options: Shared or client-carried session state instead of pinning.
Longer affinity lifetimes so remapping is rarer.
Affinity keyed on a random per-request value.
optionFeedback: Affinity is a state decision, not a free optimization.
Longer pins keep users on a degraded target for longer, which is the failure you are ending.
A random key spreads requests and destroys the affinity the design needed.
variants.hint: What does affinity cost during failover?
variants.explanation: Affinity concentrates hot keys and weakens failover predictability.

variants.title: Build the eligible set
variants.context: A proxy splits the path into separate downstream and upstream connections. Headers arriving directly from the client are untrusted; the trusted edge strips reserved identity fields and writes canonical values; later hops accept them only from known peers.
variants.prompt: A backend passes its readiness check but its queue is hidden and deep. What can the balancer do?
options: Passive outlier ejection from observed behavior.
Trust the readiness check the backend reports.
Send more traffic so the backend warms up.
optionFeedback: Observed errors and latency reveal what a readiness probe cannot.
Readiness is a self-report, and this backend reports healthy while its queue grows.
More traffic deepens a queue that is already hidden and long.
variants.hint: What evidence does the balancer have beyond the probe?
variants.explanation: Build one eligible set from discovery, readiness, and observed behavior.

variants.title: Build the eligible set
variants.context: A proxy splits the path into separate downstream and upstream connections. Headers arriving directly from the client are untrusted; the trusted edge strips reserved identity fields and writes canonical values; later hops accept them only from known peers.
variants.prompt: A zone fails and the balancer reroutes everything to the remaining zone with no reserve. What happens?
options: Latency improves as the pool concentrates.
The surviving zone overloads without reserved capacity.
Nothing; the balancer spreads the load evenly.
optionFeedback: Concentrating the same work on fewer targets raises queueing, so latency rises.
Distribution alone is not enough without capacity headroom.
Even distribution over half the capacity is still twice the load per target.
variants.hint: Where does the rerouted traffic land?
variants.explanation: Send admitted requests inside the intended failure envelope.

variants.title: Build the eligible set
variants.context: A proxy splits the path into separate downstream and upstream connections. Headers arriving directly from the client are untrusted; the trusted edge strips reserved identity fields and writes canonical values; later hops accept them only from known peers.
variants.prompt: Retries at the balancer multiply during an outage. Which control bounds them?
options: Disabling health checks during the outage.
A retry budget shared across attempts.
Unlimited retries with added jitter.
optionFeedback: Health checks are not what multiplies attempts; without them the balancer retries into dead targets.
A budget keeps retries from overloading the pool.
Jitter spreads retries in time. Without a budget the total attempts still multiply.
variants.hint: What stops retries from becoming a storm?
variants.explanation: Retry only where the contract allows, under an aggregate budget.
